item.title: Americans Increasingly See Strains in U.S.-Germany Ties as Germans Remain Pessimistic
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear and detailed analysis

The 10th annual joint survey of the American and German publics by Pew Research Center and Körber-Stiftung finds that views of the two countries’ relationship continue to cool among Americans, while Germans remain deeply pessimistic about the current state of bilateral affairs.

One-third of Americans now say the relationship between the United States and Germany is bad, the highest such measure in a decade of surveys. Still, 62% of Americans say the relationship is good, though that’s down from 71% in 2025 and 84% in 2024.

Democrats and independents who lean toward the Democratic Party drive much of this decline. In 2024, during the Biden administration, 91% of Democrats said relations with Germany were good. But in 2025, that figure dropped to 65% and it stands at 51% today.

Among Republicans and Republican leaners, 76% now say relations are good, statistically similar to the share in 2025 (81%) but down since 2024 (84%).

Germans, for their part, remain deeply skeptical of the countries’ current relations, with 21% saying they are good and 77% saying they are bad. These attitudes are similar to what they were early in the first Trump administration.

And while there are partisan divides in Germany on a variety of topics related to foreign policy – especially between Alternative for Germany (AfD) supporters and nonsupporters – Germans are relatively aligned in the view that relations with the U.S. are bad.

Are the U.S. and Germany seen as partners on global issues?

In the past few years, fewer Americans and Germans see their countries as partners on various international issues.

- Free trade: 54% of Americans say Germany is a partner on promoting free trade, down from 72% in 2023. Around a quarter of Germans (23%) say the U.S. is a partner on free trade, similar to what we found last year but down from 65% in the Biden era.

- War in Ukraine: 47% of Americans see Germany as a partner on this issue, down from 64% in 2023. About a third of Germans (35%) see the U.S. as a partner. As recently as 2023, about two-thirds of Americans and Germans said their nations were partners in dealing with the war Ukraine.

- China: 45% of Americans see Germany as a partner on China policy, down from 60% in 2023. A quarter of Germans see the U.S. as a partner in dealing with China, down from about half in 2024 (49%).

- Iran: 33% of Americans see Germany as a partner in dealing with Iran, down from 56% in 2020. The share of Germans who see the U.S. as a partner on Iran policy has shrunk as well, from 45% in 2020 to 15% today. (The 2026 surveys were conducted in September, following U.S.-Israeli military action in Iran that began in February.)

- Artificial intelligence: Newly asked this year, 43% of Americans and a quarter of Germans say the other nation is a partner in regulating AI.

Which nation is their most important foreign policy partner?

Another longstanding question on this survey asks which country is the most important partner for U.S. and German foreign policy.

Views among Germans

Attitudes in Germany are similar to last year, with 40% of Germans naming France as their most important foreign policy partner and another 24% naming the U.S. China, the European Union and Russia sit at 4% each.

Prior to the second Trump administration, most Germans said the U.S. was their most essential partner.

Most mainstream party supporters, including those who support the governing coalition – comprised of the Christian Democratic Union of Germany and the Christian Social Union in Bavaria, or CDU/CSU, and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) – as well as supporters of the Greens and the Left Party (Die Linke) say France is Germany’s most important parter.

Supporters of Alternative for Germany (AfD), however, are more likely to name the U.S. as their most important partner, ranking France second. AfD supporters also have more positive views of Russia than supporters of other parties, and 10% name Russia as their top partner – a much higher share than other groups.

Views among Americans

In the U.S., 13% name Canada as their most important partner, nearly double the amount who said the same last year (7%) and approximately tripled from 3% in 2024.

Previously, the United Kingdom was typically seen as the United States’ top partner by a large margin. In this year’s survey, 12% name the U.K., 11% name Israel and 8% name China. Only 1% of Americans say Germany is their top partner.

Democrats are far more likely than Republicans to name Canada as their top partner, while Republicans are more likely than Democrats to name Israel. This pattern conforms with other recent Center research on partisans’ views toward those countries.

Related: How Do Americans Feel About G20 Countries?

Germans are down on the ‘West’

The Germany survey also included more hypothetical questions about Germany’s reliance on the U.S. for national security and the future of the “West.” Among these findings:

- 61% of Germans say they can’t rely on the U.S. nuclear umbrella to protect their country in event of a war; 69% instead want a French or British nuclear umbrella.

- 13% want Germany to acquire its own nuclear weapons, while 86% do not.

- 35% favor Germany taking on a military leadership role in Europe, while 64% oppose this.

- 61% say Western unity – the concept of political and cultural linkage between the U.S. and Europe – no longer exists. Around four-in-ten (37%) say this unity still exists.

Which nations are seen to pose security concerns?

Americans remain more concerned, on balance, than their German counterparts about security threats from other countries.

- China: 58% of Americans say China is a major threat to their nation’s security, compared with 7% among Germans. Republicans are 10 percentage points more likely than Democrats to describe China this way (64% vs. 54%).…

Source: Pew Research Center | Published: 2026-11-23 22:47 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/11/23/americans-increasingly-see-strains-in-us-germany-ties/

item.title: Tajikistan Is Leaving the ICC
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail on international relations

Two months after Dushanbe signaled that it was looking to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), Tajikistan has officially started down that road.

Under Article 127 of the Rome Statute, the 1998 international treaty that established the permanent ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, written notification to the U.N. secretary general is required for a state to withdraw. Tajikistan delivered that notification on November 20, following the adoption of a resolution on October 1 by the lower house of the country’s parliament.

Per the Rome Statue, the withdrawal will go into effect one year after notification.

Tajikistan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Idibek Kalandar reportedly criticized the ICC for becoming an “instrument of political pressure,” echoing critiques aired by countries such as Russia, China, and Israel. The United States, under the administration of Donald Trump, has embarked on an open campaign against the ICC, including a February 2025 executive order imposing sanctions against the court and several rounds of individual designations targeting the court’s officials.

The United States, Russia, and Israel, three of the ICC’s biggest critics, signed the Rome Statute but never ratified the treaty. China never signed on.

To date, only two countries have fully withdrawn from the court: Burundi in 2017 and the Philippines in 2019. In June 2026, a trio of African states – Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali – notified the U.N. of their intention to withdraw. Chad and Venezuela sent their notifications in July, and the tiny Pacific state of Nauru did so in September.

On November 23, the presidency of the ICC’s governing body (the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute) issued a statement lamenting Tajikistan’s decision. The statement remarked that the choices by some states to disengage “risk undermining the collective pursuit of justice and weakening global efforts to end impunity.”

Tajikistan was the only Central Asian states to sign onto the Rome Statute, doing so in November 1998. Dushanbe ratified the treaty in May 2000.

The ICC presidency called on Tajikistan to engaged meaningfully with the body, reminding Dushanbe that members are entitled to raise concerns within the assembly. It’s not clear that Tajikistan ever did.

Kalandar, Tajikistan’s deputy foreign minister, reportedly said in October, “Recent assessments of the International Criminal Court’s activities indicate that this international institution systematically deviates from recognized international standards and key principles of judicial impartiality.”

Tajik officials have not specifically stated what prompted the withdrawal. But one piece of the puzzle is likely tied to unwelcome criticism following Dushanbe’s failure to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin in October 2025. That month, Tajikistan hosted a Russia-Central Asia summit and a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) meeting. In March 2023, the ICC had issued an arrest warrant for Putin related to the kidnapping of Ukrainian children amid Russia’s war with Ukraine.

As Kulobiddin Norov explained in an article for The Diplomat back in September:

Weeks before the visit, Tajik officials told the court they would not execute the warrant, citing head-of-state immunity, Russia’s non-membership in the ICC, and CIS commitments to guarantee the “security and unhindered movement” of visiting leaders. The ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber II rejected those arguments on March 19, 2026, and the court’s presidency referred the non-compliance finding to the Assembly of States Parties in May.

Putin has not yet been detained, in part because he avoids traveling to countries that might comply with the ICC warrant. Even countries that technically are obligated to do so have not, such as Mongolia, which hosted Putin in September 2024. Ulaanbaatar was found in breach of its Rome Statute commitments a month later as a result.

Mongolia, it should be noted, has not sought to withdraw from the Rome Statute.

As Norov noted the September article, Dushanbe’s interest in leaving the ICC may have a more direct trigger:

On April 10, 2025, Freedom for Eurasia, the Ukrainian Fund of International Volunteers, and the banned Islamic Renaissance Party (IRPT), represented by French lawyer Nicolas Ligneul, filed an Article 15 communication with the ICC. The filing organizations say it documents killings, torture, sexual violence, enforced disappearances, and forced exile between 2002 and 2024, and asks prosecutors to examine the responsibility of senior officials, including President Emomali Rahmon. Their chosen start date for communication is the day the ICC statute took effect in Tajikistan.

Although Putin has evaded an ICC warrant for several years, not every target of the court has been so successful. Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte was arrested on March 11, 2025 in the Philippines days after the ICC issued a warrant related to his government’s violent anti-drug campaign. Duterte had led his own personal, and preemptive, war against the ICC back in 2018 when the court began examining allegations of crimes against humanity. Last month he was found fit to stand trial.

Although the Philippines exited the court in 2019, withdrawal does not remove past commitments. In the words of the ICC’s presidency, in its letter of concern regarding Tajikistan, “The Presidency recalls that withdrawal from the Rome Statute does not relieve a State Party of obligations arising during the period in which it remained a Party to the Statute.”

All that to say: even if Tajikistan withdraws from the ICC, the ICC could still pursue a future case against Tajik officials for crimes committed during Tajikistan’s time as a member.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-23 18:28 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/tajikistan-is-leaving-the-icc/

item.title: Can the China-Russia-US Summit Turn Political Momentum Into Nuclear Risk Reduction?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, analysis of international summit

On November 19, an groundbreaking meeting between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin took place on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in Shenzhen. Described as a potential Yalta Conference by Putin, the summit produced a four-point “Declaration Toward Peace,” in which the fourth point explicitly “reaffirmed” the three major nuclear powers’ position that a “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” It also committed China, Russia, and the United States to “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”

Experts have been cautious and realistic about the prospects of achieving a major breakthrough in arms control, articulating that progress would require more than one meeting. That said, the Shenzhen summit offered a renewed political opening for cooperation and dialogue among the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Indeed, the importance of continual talks was underscored by all three leaders and best summarized by Trump’s statement: “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Denuclearization might be subject for a further engagement, as it was high up on Trump’s agenda for the trilateral summit. Yet, despite Xi’s reiteration that nuclear weapons should be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, China has remained resistant to joining arms control agreements with Russia and the United States, citing the disparity in the size of their nuclear arsenal. As a result, Trump has acknowledged that limiting nuclear weapons would be hard.

Nevertheless, considering Trump’s remark that China, Russia, and the United States are “uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons and lowering the risk of nuclear use,” the present impasse in nuclear arms reduction may suggest that greater priority should be placed on the agenda of nuclear risk reduction. Indeed, the three presidents have agreed to open a dialogue on “reducing nuclear risks.”

This momentum creates a new and unprecedented political opening among the three major powers that must be capitalized on. A more substantive agenda for nuclear risk reduction would have to be constructed to advance this political breakthrough. Specifically, subsequent meetings can be anchored on translating the political understanding and consensus for nuclear risk reduction into practical measures that can reduce the possibility of nuclear miscalculation and inadvertent escalation. Xi has even underscored that dialogues and consultation should “ensure that misjudgements occur less.”

An immediate and clear area where the three states can work together would be a joint ballistic missile launch notification agreement, precisely because such agreements are not new. A joint notification system would present an achievable and feasible topic for nuclear risk reduction, as existing arrangements provide a working foundation. Russia already signed separate notification agreements with the United States and China in 1988 and 2009 respectively. China, although not in any formal arrangements with Washington., demonstrated a willingness to provide advance notification when it informed its U.S. counterparts of its two recent launches in September 2024 and in July 2026 (although China offered short notice for the 2026 launch).

These established precedents attest that a trilateral notification arrangement may now be a realistic subject for further discussion. As such, it is only natural that the three nuclear powers explore a trilateral arrangement for advance notification of ballistic missile launches, and discuss the nature, standards, and content of notifications, all within the frame of nuclear risk reduction dialogues.

Beyond a joint launch notification arrangement, subsequent rounds of trilateral meetings can also address other pressing areas of nuclear risks, such as Xi’s recommended focus on “crisis communication and prevention mechanisms.” The maintenance of military hotlines and advance launch notifications of military exercises or activities could also help alleviate uncertainty surrounding military activities, particularly during periods of heightened tensions. In any case, feasible areas that might lessen doubt and offer predictability could provide a proper foundation for subsequent negotiations and talks.

Focusing on the practical arrangements that mitigate the risk of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation leading to a nuclear war would have several merits agreeable to all three nuclear powers. First, none of the three powers would have to explicitly commit to limiting their respective arsenals. Given the major complications of getting China and Russia to discuss arms control, coupled with the tremendous psychological difficulty and pressure that surrounds giving up nuclear weapons once a state has it, discussions on reducing or limiting nuclear weapons would be unlikely. Discussing nuclear risks and escalation would be more politically palatable, as none of the nuclear powers would have to accept any hard limits. It would still allow them to address the dangers associated with nuclear weapons while without requiring major changes to their respective nuclear force structures, doctrines, or arsenal sizes.

Second, focusing on reducing nuclear miscalculation and inadvertent escalation as the basis for dialogue would operationalize the shared responsibility of strategic stability the leaders acknowledged at the summit. Establishing arrangements that improve communication, reduce ambiguity, and lower the likelihood of miscalculation would not only provide substantive meaning to the joint declarations but it offers a clear signal that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow are responsible powers that could cooperate on matters of shared security even when the three countries remain at odds in terms of their strategic interests.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-23 17:39 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/can-the-china-russia-us-summit-turn-political-momentum-into-nuclear-risk-reduction/

item.title: Could the Jensen Huang Scandal Help China’s AI Industry?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, analysis of technology and geopolitical implications

The past few weeks have been a tough test the world’s most important tech firm, Nvidia. Huang’s departure sparked worries about Nvidia’s future as a top investor and the world’s dominant chip provider – so much so that Nvidia reinstalled him as CEO less than two weeks later.

Beyond the controversy itself, the episode exposes deeper contradictions in U.S. technology strategy. One important question is what Beijing will gain from the U.S. response to the Nvidia scandal.

As a close associate of U.S. President Donald Trump, Huang has held an influential position in U.S. technology policy toward China. He has repeatedly argued that restricting Chinese access to U.S. chips would cede a substantial market to competitors while encouraging Beijing to develop domestic alternatives. He had been the biggest advocate for selling chips to China, which he argued helps the United States maintain its market dominance.

The scandal that enveloped Huang thus takes on geopolitical significance. Even with his reinstatement at CEO, his political standing has taken a hit.

Bipartisan efforts to tighten semiconductor controls are expected to significantly advance. The competing view on export controls argues that Washington needs to secure strategic advantage through technological restrictions. The proposed MATCH Act and Remote Access Security Act (RASA), for instance, reflect the expanding scope of this debate. Already, the Trump administration has announced new restrictions on chips sales to third countries and Chinese access to data centers abroad that use U.S. technology.

Another tech transfer route that features prominently in the debates among U.S. policymakers is open-weight models. Huang was one of Silicon Valley’s most powerful champions of open models, where Chinese firms have concentrated their bets. He defended distillation, which means training one model on the output of another. Washington is actively weighing transparency rules and targeted bans aimed specifically at Chinese open-weight models. Huang’s diminished standing will strengthen those advocating for proprietary systems, who fear that cheaper Chinese models could undermine their profitability.

Bipartisan score settling in the United States adds to the existing uncertainty over AI regulation, open-source development, and the commercial interests of U.S. technology companies. This could create strategic openings for Beijing to exploit.

On one hand, tighter restrictions could further strengthen China’s resolve to innovate independently. As Washington’s restrictions on exports to Chinese vendors grow, the immediate beneficiaries would be Chinese semiconductor manufacturers and domestic suppliers seeking to capture demand previously directed toward Nvidia. More importantly, restrictions could create a larger and more predictable domestic market for these firms. Chinese AI developers would have stronger incentives to optimize models for domestic processors, collaborate with local chipmakers, and invest in alternative computing architectures.

Herein, Huawei and Alibaba could be direct beneficiaries. Experts and industry specialists have argued that Washington’s earlier restrictions on semiconductor exports reinforced Beijing’s determination to build a more self-sufficient industrial ecosystem. A further tightening of controls following the Huang controversy could accelerate this trajectory.

On the other hand, Huang’s scandal – and Nvidia’s revamped compliance structures – could remove a critical commercial link between China and the United States. This would directly dampen China’s access to Nvidia chips, which remain the world’s most advanced. More importantly, building self-sufficiency in Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) does not reduce China’s reliance on U.S. technology. Nvidia’s most critical technology is the software, Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), which Chinese models significantly rely on. Most models cannot run CUDA without compatible Nvidia chips.

The uncertainty in the U.S. tech industry leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next. Since the first export control measures were implemented, Chinese chipmakers have been increasingly relying on third-party cloud firms and shell companies in East Asian countries. Alice Huang, with whom Huang is alleged to have an affair, earlier served as an executive of a Singapore-based data center firm, Megaspeed, which has been accused of helping Chinese firms access Nvidia chips.

Control over data centers in Southeast Asia is set to become a new dimension in China-U.S. technology competition. More precisely, regulating data centers in a third country may become a priority in U.S. AI policy. It could also put a dent in long-term ties between East Asia and U.S. technology ecosystems. Huang’s scandal has attracted immense attention to the role of Southeast Asian firms, in particular, in export controls. That will make it harder for Southeast Asian companies to access U.S. advanced chips, even for domestic use.

As the U.S. tech ecosystem becomes unpredictable and grows more restrictive to other countries, it creates more space for China to diversify its technology partnerships, especially in Southeast Asian countries. China can present itself as a proponent of technological cooperation, with its low-cost, open-source models, and could gain greater influence in developing countries. This may provide a window of opportunity for China to close the gap with the United States in computing capacity.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-23 15:53 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, analysis of space race and technology

go beyond the headlines.

November 23, 2026

Topher Haddad and Ryan P. Nelson

A new front in the U.S.-Chinese space race is emerging in the lowest reaches of space: very low Earth orbit, the untapped orbital regime below 320 kilometers. There, China is laying the groundwork for a significant presence, with announced plans for more than 2,200 satellites and an aggressive deployment timeline through 2030.

Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellites from debris and nuclear radiation that could disable spacecraft in higher orbits, making China’s space architecture more resilient.

These are strategic advantages the United States should be prepared to counter. The answer is not to match China satellite for satellite, but to improve American space capabilities and survivability. Washington should respond by expanding orbital diversity across its space architecture, assessing where very low Earth orbit offers operational advantages worth pursuing, and working with industry to coordinate the orbit’s development.

As executives at Albedo, a U.S. startup building satellites for very low Earth orbit, we have a stake in the future of this orbital regime. We recognize that the orbit’s advantages come with trade-offs, which we discuss openly below. But our roles have given us a close-up view of its evolution from an experimental frontier into a domain of strategic competition, and we believe China’s ambitions there warrant far more attention in Washington.

Satellites operate at vastly different altitudes depending on their missions. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, geostationary Earth orbit keeps satellites over the same region for persistent communications and surveillance. Medium Earth orbit, between roughly 2,000 and 36,000 kilometers, hosts GPS and other navigation satellites. Most new satellite activity is in low Earth orbit, extending to roughly 2,000 kilometers, with most satellites above 450 kilometers. Cheaper to reach than higher orbits, low Earth orbit offers advantages for communications and remote sensing, but is increasingly crowded with satellites and debris. That crowding and the advantages of proximity have drawn both government and commercial interest to very low Earth orbit.

Very low Earth orbit refers to the orbital regime of 320 kilometers and below, where the atmosphere starts to become dense enough to both rapidly clear debris and shield satellites from radiation, benefits that grow stronger as altitude decreases. Since these altitudes lie within the upper atmosphere, drag and atomic oxygen have historically made sustained operations difficult. Though advances in propulsion technology, surface materials, and spacecraft design are now overcoming these challenges, operating so close to Earth still comes with trade-offs. Satellites must expend power thrusting against drag, and while purpose-built designs can support lifespans of around five years, those lifespans can vary as solar activity changes atmospheric density. Another trade-off is coverage: each satellite sees less of Earth, requiring more satellites for broader coverage.

Where proximity to Earth matters, however, very low Earth orbit can bring significant benefits. Remote sensing satellites can achieve substantially higher resolution, helping operators more precisely track military forces on Earth. Proximity also brings stronger communications signals and lower latency, useful for tactical missions at the edge.

Very low Earth orbit also offers distinct resiliency and sustainability advantages. Because the atmosphere is roughly 100 times denser than in higher low Earth orbit, debris that would remain in low Earth orbit for years clears from very low Earth orbit in days to weeks, reducing collision risks for satellites. That same atmosphere provides natural shielding against persistent radiation effects of an orbital nuclear detonation, should one occur during a conflict. This would allow satellites to remain operational even if radiation disrupts those in higher orbits.

The orbit’s economics differ, too. Drag can raise operating and replenishment costs. But smaller, cheaper payloads can match or exceed the performance of larger ones higher up. And for missions requiring protection against nuclear effects, the orbit’s natural shielding avoids hardening costs that would be prohibitively expensive for constellations in higher orbits.

It is these benefits that have made very low Earth orbit a growing priority within China’s space plans. Since 2022, China has successfully operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in very low Earth orbit, proving its ability to sustain satellites there. China is now building on those demonstrations with plans to deploy very low Earth orbit constellations at a scale unmatched by any other government.

Publicly announced Chinese plans project more than 2,200 very low Earth orbit satellites, spanning remote sensing, communications, and computing missions. With only about a dozen total satellites operating at these altitudes today, such a buildout would transform very low Earth orbit into a proliferated layer of China’s space infrastructure. The timeline is uncertain, but the trajectory is clear. One senior member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering — the nation’s top engineering academy — recently called the next five years a “critical window” for China in very low Earth orbit, and that the country “must complete the transition from technology experimentation to large-scale application.”…

item.title: The Double Alignment Problem: Civil-Military Relations in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, analysis of civil-military relations and AI

go beyond the headlines.

November 23, 2026

Theo Lipsky

Artificial intelligence poses the greatest challenge to American civil-military relations since the advent of the nuclear bomb. AI plays outside the political bounds that contain other challenges, however odious. It compounds the inherent problem of civil-military relations – aligning the state and the military – with an additional alignment problem: that of human and agent. In doing so, AI threatens to undermine the constitutionalism and professionalism on which status quo civil-military relations depend. Nonetheless, artificial intelligence has developed so fast that the field of civil-military relations lags far behind it.

What follows is an attempt to reckon with the implications of AI for civil-military relations. For though in important ways AI is without technological precedent, its development is not the first time that a society has had to develop means of controlling an alien, useful and sometimes inscrutable body capable of great destruction. These parallels suggest ways of mitigating the risks to civil-military relations posed by this double-alignment problem.

Societies have long struggled to prevent misalignment with their militaries. The military profession survived such conflagrations because technology and geopolitics both necessitated it, but the question of how to mitigate the risk they represent has endured. In 1957, Samuel Huntington proposed an answer he called “objective control,” wherein the state granted a military great autonomy and a more centralized chain of command in exchange for categorical subordination to the constitutional system. Per Huntington, this arrangement would benefit from a more centralized chain of command than the Constitution provided, a more conservative society, and an evolved sense of professionalism.

Though Huntington’s model came to dominate the new volunteer military’s conception of its relationship with the state, American society did not heed his calls to grow more conservative, nor did the state heed his calls for it to unify military command under the Executive. Instead, as his student Peter Feaver pointed out, the military labored under sustained and intrusive monitoring throughout the Cold War – and largely complied. To explain as much, Feaver reframed the civil-military relationship problem as one of society’s great principal-agent problems. Society’s task was to author codes and norms that incentivized the agent to behave.

Just as civil-military theory was coming into its own, elsewhere in American society ideas about a new alignment problem were emerging. In 1960, Norbert Wiener theorized that novel “learning machines” might threaten harm through misalignment. In the ensuing decades, the development of those machines proceeded unevenly, but the alignment problem Wiener suggested was not forgotten. Nick Bostrom’s influential 2003 paper argued that a superintelligent machine without an adequately encoded and benevolent “supergoal” might pursue subordinate tasks in dangerous fashion. Present leaders in the field have enunciated the alignment problem and proposed solutions, one calling it the “core problem of AI research.” Much as Peter Feaver did for civil-military relations, researchers now propose multi-agent AI be understood as a principal-agent problem.

Parallels are evident. Both the military and AI have the power to do great harm to the society they serve. Both claim significant autonomy is needed to fulfill their value proposition. Both labor under dual imperatives to be effective and to keep society’s values in view. Both are complex and opaque enough to pose monitoring challenges to the society they serve. Both largely evaluate themselves in training. Both invoke geopolitical risks to move so fast that monitors struggle to keep up.

A double alignment problem thus arises from the integration of AI into military affairs. That double alignment problem poses a unique threat to civil-military relations. Other threats concerning personnel decisions or war authorities are important, but they can be reduced to a contest between known human agents within the bounds of a Constitutional system. For all their ugliness, such threats are knowable. The agents that will soon manage violence for the state do not exist within the Constitutional system, as we’ll see. And as of now, they are to the state and military alike largely unknown.

We now turn to the ways we might understand these problems suggested by their parallel attributes. Huntington’s use of constitutionalism and professionalism provides a ready starting point not only for the categorization of risks posed by the double alignment problem but for the mitigation of them.

At the heart of Huntington’s solution to the civil-military alignment problem – “objective control” – is the military’s professionalism, a central feature of which is the military’s responsibility to the Constitution. Huntington might have found that Constitution ill-suited for his preferred “objective control,” but he ceded that it did much to professionalize the military. The agents of the military take iterative oaths to that constitution. Their institution is funded and regulated by a constitutional legislature. They are confirmed individually for positions of high responsibility by that legislature, and take orders from a constitutional executive.…

Why it is here: original reporting, methodology of survey research

The American Trends Panel survey methodology

Overview

Data in this report comes from Wave 203 of the American Trends Panel (ATP), Pew Research Center’s nationally representative panel of randomly selected U.S. adults. 15, 2026. A total of 10,247 panelists responded out of 11,574 who were sampled, for a survey-level response rate of 89%.

The cumulative response rate accounting for nonresponse to the recruitment surveys and attrition is 3%. The break-off rate among panelists who logged on to the survey and completed at least one item is 1%. The margin of sampling error for the full sample of 10,247 respondents is plus or minus 1.3 percentage points.

SSRS conducted the survey for Pew Research Center via online (n=9,910) and live telephone (n=337) interviewing. Interviews were conducted in both English and Spanish.

To learn more about the ATP, read “About the American Trends Panel.”

Panel recruitment

Since 2018, the ATP has used address-based sampling (ABS) for recruitment. A study cover letter and a pre-incentive are mailed to a stratified, random sample of households selected from the U.S. Postal Service’s Computerized Delivery Sequence File. This Postal Service file has been estimated to cover 90% to 98% of the population.1 Within each sampled household, the adult with the next birthday is selected to participate. Other details of the ABS recruitment protocol have changed over time but are available upon request.2 Prior to 2018, the ATP was recruited using landline and cellphone random-digit-dial surveys administered in English and Spanish.

A national sample of U.S. adults has been recruited to the ATP approximately once per year since 2014. In some years, the recruitment has included additional efforts (known as an “oversample”) to improve the accuracy of data for underrepresented groups. For example, Hispanic adults, Black adults and Asian adults were oversampled in 2019, 2022 and 2023, respectively.

Sample design

The overall target population for this survey was noninstitutionalized persons ages 18 and older living in the United States. All active panel members were invited to participate in this wave.

Questionnaire development and testing

The questionnaire was developed by Pew Research Center in consultation with SSRS. The web program used for online respondents was rigorously tested on both PC and mobile devices by the SSRS project team and Pew Research Center researchers. The SSRS project team also populated test data that was analyzed in SPSS to ensure the logic and randomizations were working as intended before launching the survey.

Incentives

All respondents were offered a post-paid incentive for their participation. Respondents could choose to receive the post-paid incentive in the form of a check or gift code to Amazon.com, Target.com or Walmart.com. Incentive amounts ranged from $5 to $20 depending on whether the respondent belongs to a part of the population that is harder or easier to reach. Differential incentive amounts were designed to increase panel survey participation among groups that traditionally have low survey response propensities.

Data collection protocol

The data collection field period for this survey was Nov. 9 to 15, 2026. Surveys were conducted via self-administered web survey or by live telephone interviewing.

For panelists who take surveys online:3 Postcard notifications were mailed to a subset on Nov. 9.4 Survey invitations were sent out in two separate launches: soft launch and full launch. Sixty panelists were included in the soft launch, which began with an initial invitation sent on Nov. 9. All remaining English- and Spanish-speaking sampled online panelists were included in the full launch and were sent an invitation on Nov. 10.

Panelists participating online were sent an email invitation and up to two email reminders if they did not respond to the survey. ATP panelists who consented to SMS messages were sent an SMS invitation with a link to the survey and up to two SMS reminders.

For panelists who take surveys over the phone with a live interviewer: Prenotification postcards were mailed on Nov. 6. Soft launch took place on Nov. 9 and involved dialing until a total of eight interviews had been completed. All remaining English- and Spanish-speaking sampled phone panelists’ numbers were dialed throughout the remaining field period. Panelists who take surveys via phone can receive up to six calls from trained SSRS interviewers.

Data quality checks

To ensure high-quality data, Center researchers performed data quality checks to identify any respondents showing patterns of satisficing. This includes checking for whether respondents left questions blank at very high rates or always selected the first or last answer presented. As a result of this checking, three ATP respondents were removed from the survey dataset prior to weighting and analysis.

Use of artificial intelligence (AI)

Survey responses to some open-ended questions were initially coded using AI-assisted text classification. Human researchers reviewed, validated, and, where necessary, corrected AI-generated codes prior to analysis.

Weighting

The ATP data is weighted in a process that accounts for multiple stages of sampling and nonresponse that occur at different points in the panel survey process. First, each panelist begins with a base weight that reflects their probability of recruitment into the panel. These weights are then calibrated to align with the population benchmarks in the accompanying table to correct for nonresponse to recruitment surveys and panel attrition.
